# Consumer Tech Documentation (WDIII Tech Vault)
> Real-world experiments, empirical hardware benchmarks, and documented consumer tech findings across repair, customer service, software performance, hardware teardowns, ecosystem integrations, and mobile AI.

- **Author**: WDIII
- **Version**: v6.3
- **Last Updated**: October 8, 2026
- **Status**: Live Independent Research Archive

## Overview
The WDIII Tech Vault documents rigorous, firsthand, empirical testing of consumer electronic hardware and operating systems under controlled laboratory and real-world conditions. **Version 6.3 (v6.3)** introduces the complete Opus 5.5 "Bench Notes" visual language overhaul with bespoke typography (Bricolage Grotesque and Instrument Sans), elevated paper card structures, comprehensive security headers with strict CSP and sandbox controls, accessibility enhancements, route announcements, global rate limiting, input focus improvements, updated light theme styling, verified Experiment 9 hardware details and metrics, refreshed methodologies, expanded hardware datasets, unified measurement schemas, and verified empirical verdicts. Every experiment includes explicit methodology, test parameters, quantitative measurements, observations, and conclusive verdicts.

## Official Experiments & Findings

### Experiment 1: Apple vs Samsung Mail-In Repair
- **Category**: Repair | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: iPhone 17 Pro Max, Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra
- **Objective**: Compare official manufacturer mail-in repair turnaround, total cost, customer communication, and physical repair quality for identical level 9 cracked screen damage.
- **Results**: Apple completed repair in 2 days at $600 with pristine quality and proactive communication. Samsung took ~1 month ($289–$300) due to a 14-day administrative failure where an incorrect email address delayed the payment link, requiring a full re-dispatch, though physical repair quality was also pristine.
- **Verdict**: Winner: Apple. Apple charges double ($600 vs $300) but delivers in 2 days with zero friction. Samsung's administrative failure erased every cost advantage.

### Experiment 2: Repair Channel Comparison
- **Category**: Repair | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: 3 identical iPhone 15s with identical level 9 screen and back-glass damage (one per channel)
- **Objective**: Compare Official Apple, a third-party shop using genuine parts, and a cheap unauthorized shop using generic parts on cost, turnaround, quality, waterproofing and warranty.
- **Results**: Official Apple charged $399 (8 days in total), with a pristine result and waterproofing kept. The genuine-parts third party quoted $450 with no quality checks or warranty, then couldn't source parts, so the repair was cancelled before any work was done. The cheap unauthorized shop charged $220 with a 1-day turnaround, but used generic parts, super-glued the back glass (losing waterproofing), fitted a noticeably thicker screen and gave no warranty.
- **Verdict**: Winner: Official Apple ($399, 8 days total), the only option that preserved waterproofing, warranty and part authenticity.

### Experiment 3: Customer Service Quality Test
- **Category**: Support | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Objective**: Ask phone support at 8 smartphone brands the same question ("My phone screen is going black"; the correct answer is that the battery is draining and needs charging) and score speed to the correct answer, troubleshooting quality, accuracy and helpfulness.
- **Results**: Huawei 4.5/5, Xiaomi 4.5/5, OPPO 3.5/5, OnePlus 3/5, Apple 2.5/5, Vivo 1/5, Samsung 0/5, BlackBerry 0/5. Vivo answered quickly but wouldn't help and offered email instead; Samsung's automated system hung up; BlackBerry required a fee to speak to a human.
- **Verdict**: Winners: Huawei & Xiaomi (tied at 4.5/5). One call per brand, so anecdotal rather than a statistical sample.

### Experiment 4: iOS Performance Comparison (Historical)
- **Category**: Software | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: iPhone 15 Pro
- **Objective**: Compare iOS 18.6 and iOS 26.0.1 on the same iPhone 15 Pro, following iOS 26 through to 26.4.2.
- **Results**: iOS 26 was faster in every performance test (boot, storage transfer, 8–13% faster app loading, browser benchmarks) but had lower 3DMark thermal stability (70.9% vs 88.4%) and worse battery (66% vs 74% remaining on the same workload at 26.0.1, 71% by 26.4.2).
- **Verdict**: iOS 26 is the better OS, but only after the dust settled several months post-launch. Wait for the .2 or .3 release before updating a daily driver.

### Case Study: Samsung Battery Failures & Corporate Accountability
- **Category**: Legal / Hardware | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Objective**: Document battery swelling in stored Samsung devices from 2016–2020, Samsung's response, the escalation and the outcome.
- **Results**: Seven devices swelled (Galaxy S8, S10, S10e, Note 8 ×2, Z Fold 2, S20 FE); newer Galaxy S21–S26 models, non-Samsung devices and an iPhone 5c in the same storage did not. The S20 FE failed at 18 months against Samsung's own 5-year battery claim. After 50 days without a substantive response and complaints to the CPSC and BBB plus a consumer rights attorney, Samsung settled on June 18.
- **Verdict**: $1,020 cash settlement across 7 devices, no NDA.

### Experiment 5: Battery Life — Google Pixel Pro vs iPhone
- **Category**: Hardware | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: Pixel 6 Pro, Pixel 7 Pro, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 9 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro, iPhone 13, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 16e (all on brand-new batteries)
- **Objective**: Compare real-world screen-on time and daily endurance rather than synthetic benchmarks.
- **Results**: The Pixel 10 Pro and iPhone 16e tied at about 1.5 days. The Pixel 9 Pro, with the smallest battery (4700 mAh), came 2nd among the Pixels, well ahead of the 5003 mAh Pixel 6 Pro.
- **Verdict**: Winner: Pixel 10 Pro & iPhone 16e (tied, ~1.5 days). Chip efficiency beats raw battery capacity.

### Experiment 6: AASP Repair Test — iFix
- **Category**: Repair | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: iPhone 16 Pro Max with level 9 screen and back-glass damage (data contributed by MTA)
- **Objective**: Test whether an Apple Authorized Service Provider (iFix) delivers Official Apple repair quality, the channel missing from Experiment 2.
- **Results**: $599, with quality identical to Official Apple: the same warranty extension, no defects, and waterproofing and parts authentication preserved. Costs aren't directly comparable with Experiment 2, which used an iPhone 15.
- **Verdict**: An AASP is a legitimate alternative to Official Apple when an Apple Store isn't accessible.

### Experiment 7: Google Pixel Pro Generation Comparison
- **Category**: Hardware | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Devices Tested**: Pixel 6 Pro through Pixel 10 Pro (Tensor G1–G5), one unit per generation
- **Objective**: Compare five Pixel Pro generations on chips, cameras and real-world performance.
- **Results**: Tensor G1–G4, made on Samsung processes, throttled under heavy use; the TSMC-made G5 in the 10 Pro runs cooler and didn't throttle during long video recording. Camera megapixel counts have stayed the same since the 7 Pro, and the biggest gains came from processing.
- **Verdict**: Buy the 10 Pro, keep the 8 Pro, skip the rest.

### Experiment 8: Cross-Platform Ecosystem Reliability & Hardware Longevity
- **Category**: Ecosystem | **Status**: In Progress (protocol v1.0 approved 2026-09-27; day 0 and week 0 recorded 2026-09-27; no analysis yet)
- **Objective**: Track cross-device feature reliability (clipboard sync, file transfer, phone-to-watch notifications, earbud audio switching) and hardware longevity for Apple, Google and Samsung, with a phone, laptop, watch and earbuds each, over 24 months.

### Experiment 9: Comprehensive Apple Ecosystem Security Audit
- **Category**: Software | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Target Hardware**: iPhone 16e (iOS 27.0 beta), iPhone 13 (iOS 26.5), MacBook Air host (macOS Tahoe 26.x, model TBD)
- **Objective**: Hands-on audit of the Apple consumer ecosystem across 13 threat scenarios in three phases (authentication and recovery, Find My and tracking, local wireless), 2026-08-07 to 2026-09-09.

### Experiment 10: Year-Long iOS 26 vs iOS 27 Survey on iPhone 16e
- **Category**: Software | **Status**: Paused (phase A on iOS 26 collected but not yet in the data log; phase B on iOS 27 not started; no comparison made)
- **Target Hardware**: iPhone 16e (one device, before/after design; separate from Experiment 12)
- **Objective**: Compare standby battery drain, built-in app launch times and stability on the same iPhone 16e before (iOS 26) and after (iOS 27) the major update, then track iOS 27 point updates for a year.

### Experiment 11: Fast Charging Degradation & Thermals
- **Category**: Hardware | **Status**: Completed (Done)
- **Objective**: Assess 45W vs 25W vs 15W Qi charging cycles, thermals, and projected health degradation.

### Experiment 12: iOS 27 Performance & AI Chatbot Integration on iPhone 16e
- **Category**: Software / AI | **Status**: In Progress (testing underway on iOS 27.0; no results yet)
- **Target Hardware**: iPhone 16e (Model iPhone17,5), one device, in a temperature-controlled room (about 21°C); the same phone is used for Experiment 10, which keeps a separate log
- **OS Baseline**: iOS 27.0; later iOS 27 updates tracked as they are released
- **Objective**: Test Apple's iOS 27 claims on iPhone 16e, including the claimed "up to 60%" improvement in app responsiveness. Once Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT get third-party Siri support, compare all three through Siri with identical prompts.
- **Procedures**: (A) Cold and warm app launch times timed with a stopwatch, overnight standby drain, and counts of new crash logs in Analytics Data, using the same battery and stability methods as Experiment 10. (B) AI chatbots via Siri: not started, waiting for third-party support; the plan compares latency, handoff reliability and multi-turn context. (C) Headline features to verify: TBD.
- **Standalone Document**: `/experiment-12.html`

## Programmatic Fetching APIs (CORS Enabled)
All endpoints return `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for seamless cross-origin fetching by external tools, scripts, and AI agents:
- `GET /api/summary`: Complete machine-readable JSON summary of the entire archive.
- `GET /api/experiments`: Full list of all 15 experiments with measurement schemas and verdicts.
- `GET /api/experiments/:id`: Query a single experiment by ID or number (e.g. `/api/experiments/exp1`, `/api/experiments/exp12`).
- `GET /api/devices`: Hardware devices registry with specifications and benchmarks.
- `GET /api/devices/:id`: Query a single device record.
- `GET /llms.txt`: This plain-text documentation.
- `GET /`: Complete HTML single-page application.
- `GET /experiment-12.html`: Standalone Experiment 12 protocol document.
